messages.subject_clean: How can I obtain the over-dipersion parameter in r-inla?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I fitted a Poisson mixed model with “Nwrestler” as random effect. The model is overdispersed. For this reason, I obtained the Pearson dispersion parameter with the lme4 package (Phi=1.56).

For exemple with a generalized linear model:

g(%mu_i) = X'beta

where %mu_i=E(y_i) and g is the link function. The variance of y_i is:

Var(y_i)= %phi * V(%mu_i)

In the lme4 package, the estimate of dispersion is measured by both the deviance or Pearson's chi-square divided by their degrees of freedom.

When I’ve used the inla package, I've obtained the variance of random effect but I don't know how can obtain the dispersion parameter.

formula<-injuries~offset(log(combat))+Category+fallswinner+f(factor(Nwrestler),model="iid",param=c(0.001,0.001))

model5<-inla(formula,data=veranregyes,family="poisson",Ntrials=n,control.compute=list(dic=T,cpo=TRUE), control.inla=list(strategy="laplace", int.strategy="grid"))

prec.marg <- (model5$marginals.hyperpar$'Precision for factor(Nwrestler)')

marg.variance = inla.tmarginal(function(x) 1/x, prec.marg)

m = inla.emarginal(function(x) x, marg.variance)

mm = inla.emarginal(function(x) x^2, marg.variance)

print(paste("mean", m))

Do you know how can I obtain the dipersion parameter?

Thanks in advance.

Martí

> When I’ve used the inla package, I've obtained the variance of random

You don't. Spesify instead a likelihood which allow for overdispersion,
f.ex the negative binomial in your case (family = "nbinomial"). Then you
get an estimate of the overdispersion parameter in that model; see
inla.doc("nbinomial")

Another alternative, is to add a iid term to each linear predictor,
which will increase the variance. But it can be difficult to relate the
variance/precision of this term, directly to the 'dispersion parameter'
you get out from lme4.

messages.subject: Recent changes in INLA
messages.body_plain:
This email is to inform you about two recent changes in INLA, starting
from the testing-version of today.

* The internal graph-spesifcation has been under a major revision and
made more general. Plotting is easier. All is easier. The changes are
backward-compatible.

The FAQ page is updated

https://sites.google.com/a/r-inla.org/www/faq#TOC-Some-of-the-models-needs-a-graph-ho

on these new changes.  In short,

- the argument in f(), 'graph.file', is replaced by a more general
argument 'graph', but your old code will still runs, although you will
get a warning the first time. To fix this, simply replace argument
'graph.file' with 'graph'.

- You can now specify a binary neighbour (sparse) symmetric matrix as
the 'graph' instead of a storing the graph on a file. Hopefully, this
would make it easier to convert from graph-spesifications from other
packages.

* The builds for Windows 32bit machines are now done in a 32bit
(emulator) environment, using a 32bit compiler (and not any more, as
for Linux and MaxOSX, running the 64bit compiler in a 32bit mode).
Hopefully, this will improve the stability, preliminary reports are
good.

--
INLA help <he...@r-inla.org>

messages.subject_clean: Using INLA with arbitrary link functions
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I wanted to know if its possible to use INLA with an arbitrary (but smooth) link function - either as it is currently or through minor modifications of its code base ? Also, are there any theoretical restriction on the link function ?

Our group has been developing methods for finite element (FE) simulations of tissue models from imaging data - for e.g. using FE models to align two brain images acquired pre and intra-operatively with MRI. As part of this, we have been exploring techniques to characterize the posterior distributions of the FE-mesh deformations conditioned on imaging data and various imaging parameters, in order to understand their effect on the uncertainty of the models. FE-meshes exhibit Markov structure, where the effect of a deformation at one mesh vertex is restricted to only a very small neighborhood. Moreover, assuming elastic material properties, the total deformation energy of the mesh has a quadratic form, which provides a Gaussian prior distribution on mesh deformation parameters. As a result, the model takes on a GMRF form with only linear dependance on its parameters modulated through the link function  - and therefore we were interested in using INLA to study these posterior distributions. However, the link function g is the image that maps a voxel location in R^3 to R.

We would really appreciate any suggestions on how to proceed.

Thanks,
-firdaus

messages.subject: Re: basis for spde
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

> spde <-inla.spde.create(mesh, model="matern", param=list(basis.K, basis.T))

The problem here is the R syntax; inla.spde.create requires the parameters in the param list to be named, so you need
  param=list(basis.K=basis.K, basis.T=basis.T)

But be careful with your choice of basis; Spherical harmonics with order=3 gives 9 basis functions, which in turn will give you 18 hyperparameters (9 each for kappa^2 and tau) for inla to estimate, which is quite a lot!

> The second question is that I use the function “inla.spde2.matern”, I see the manual writing that B.tau and B.kappa are the matrix with specification of log-linear model. What the exact mean and requirement for formulating the matrix?

A brief mathematical definition is provided in the help text for inla.spde2.matern (more documentation is on its way...); to obtain the same model as for inla.spde.create, you can set
  B.tau=cbind(0, basis.T, basis.K*0)
  B.kappa=cbind(0, basis.T*0, basis.K/2)
The first column is an offset, and the rest are weigthed together from a common parameter vector theta.  The "/2" is there because inla.spde2.matern works with "log(kappa)", whereas inla.spde.create works with "log(kappa^2)".

/Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marc,

I'm not 100% on what's gone wrong (more of Håvard's area and he'll probably step in if I'm too wrong!), but I can explain the process and point out where it may have gone wrong.

In essence, this bit of INLA does the following:

1) Find the mode of the Laplace approximation posterior \pi(\theta|y)
2) Compute the Hessian at the mode (not computed during the optimization!)
3) Do stuff with the Hessian

Something can go wrong at the first two stages.  The optimizer may stop before it reaches the mode, which will result in the Hessian not necessarily being positive definite.  You can try to fix this by playing with the parameters of the optimization routine (try the tolerance and restart options in control.inla).

The other thing that can go wrong is that the approximate Hessian, which is computed by Finite Differences, is not sufficiently accurate.  This is changed by playing with the h parameter.

Another option is to just "help the optimizer along" by having a pilot run on an easier (but different!) model.  This is explained here: http://www.r-inla.org/?place=msg%2Fr-inla-discussion-group%2Fuf2ZGh4jmWc%2FA0rdPE5W7uMJ

Hope this helps,

Dan

messages.subject_clean: Using INLA with arbitrary link functions
messages.body_plain:
Wow! This sounds like a really interesting application!

In principle, it is not difficult to add a link function to INLA and if you have a specific form, we can probably add it for you fairly quickly.

There is one fairly important caveat: If the link function isn't monotone, there's no guarantee that pi(x|y,\theta) will be unimodal and so the Laplace approximation (as implemented) may not work very well!  In theory, every Laplace approximation could be computed as a mixture of a Gaussian approximation at each mode, however this is not handled (and will probably not be handled in the future) by our INLA code.

Hope this helps,

Dan

> I was surprised to see that under FAQs there is no way to deal with
> > missing covariates within INLA, according to the posting.

The key is the second part of the FAQ answer; "No", the r-inla interface has no general-purpose method for dealing with with missing covariates, but "Yes", if you can construct a joint model for the covariates and observations, inla can estimate it for you, just as WinBUGS would.  It just needs to be specified in terms of a generalised linear model framework.

Since the type of useful covariate prior would depend entirely on the specific application, writing a general purpose interface for this would be difficult.   E.g. an "uninformative and independent" prior would likely never be useful, since then you might as well remove the corresponding observations without loosing any information, and informative priors need to be constructed using some actual information, such as dependence between covariate values.

/Finn

On Thursday, 15 March 2012 14:35:38 UTC+1, Facundo Muñoz wrote:
>
> all.equal(1:mesh$n, which(int.idx))

> # they are exactly the first mesh$n points

> # and the vertices are exactly the same

>
> plot(mesh)
> points(mesh2$loc[int.idx, ], col='red', pch=20)

Here you implicitly made the assumption that the points are in the same _order_ in both meshes.  They are not.

The way the triangulation algorithm works is not always easily predictable.  One might think that a regular set of input points would produce a predictable output, but due to robustness considerations, points are added in different order depending on whether they are known to blong to a boundary or not.

The following comparison shows that most of the points do have the same C-diagonal values (the exception being the points on the boundary of the regular interior):

plot(1:mesh$n, sort(iw), pch=20, xlim=c(-300,300), ylim=c(0,0.01))
points(-(1:mesh$n), sort(iw2[int.idx]), col='red', pch=20)

If you want more control over a regular interior, specify a lattice (see inla.mesh.lattice) and use $idx$loc to map between your input order and the resulting order in the mesh.  Note that when a regular lattice is extended, the triangulation will not necessarily be regular in the interior, since the irregular behaviour in the extension can "creep" into the interior.  This mostly happens when max.edge is set to a value smaller than the input lattice resolution.

/Finn

Somehow, the original message seems to have disappeared, but here are some further comments:

The mesh you are using is very ill-defined, as you have simply constructed a pure Delaunay triangulation of your input points, that are very clustered, making for poor FEM numerics.  As a minimum, you should use "refine=TRUE" (to get minimum triangle angle >=21 degrees) and "cutoff=1000" ( distances closer than this are likely too short for the large-scale spatial model to handle, so don't even try; data closer together than this will be treated as having the same true spatial field value, unless you introduce an "A matrix" in the observation equation).  Also with your data scale (metres? maybe not.), to reduce the edge effects where you actually have data, I suggest setting at least "offset=20000", as "100" is _really_ small...

I would also suggest trying the newer spde2 model, as it will set a prior for log(kappa) that is appropriate for the size of your domain; this may eliminate the need for rescaling the domain.  The default parametrisation of the spde2 model is theta1=log(tau) and theta2=log(kappa).

I couldn't test the resulting code, since you didn't include your linear constraint generator, which depends on the size and location data of the mesh, which will now be slightly different (3515 instead of 3757 vertices).  The changed bits:

mesh.dummy = inla.mesh.create(loc=borders,extend=list(n=16,offset=10000),refine=FALSE)
boundary = inla.mesh.boundary(mesh.dummy)
mesh = inla.mesh.create(loc=cbind(work[,'X'],work[,'Y'], 0),boundary=boundary,
                        refine=TRUE, cutoff=1000)
nmesh = mesh$n
mesh.idx = mesh$idx$loc

## Definition of the SPDE model
spde = inla.spde2.matern(mesh=mesh, alpha=2)

/Finn L

yes, this is a recurrent theme.

if you have

	f(i, ..., constr=TRUE)

is means that

	sum(x) = 0,

say, in the model, hence we would like that

	sum( E(x | y) ) = 0

so that

	sum(result$summary.random$i$mean)

should be (close to zero). This is not necessarily so in INLA. (Well, it
will be not that far off but not zero.) This beacuse, the marginal
expectation E( x_i | y) is computed from the marginal of x_i|y which
again is computed under the model where sum(x) = 0. However, the
estimate of x_i|y is done 'independently' for each i, so we do not 'see
the sum(x)=0 constraint' a posteriori, so even though sum(x)=0 apriori,
there is not 'joint distribution' a posteriori that will ensure that
sum(x)=0 also aposteriori. We only do the best guess we can for each i.

Only if strategy="gaussian", you will get that sum(E(x|y)) = 0 (or close
to zero), as the sum(x)=0 constraint survive after conditioning on
data.

Similar for the more general constraints, Ax=e.

On Monday, 19 March 2012 19:02:51 UTC+1, Virgilio Gómez-Rubio wrote:
> Many thanks for your replies. It may be a good idea to report NA's in summary.fitted.values Also,
> I set family=beta in the call to inla(), so I supposed that inla() knew that my responses are beta
> distributed...

 Yes, in principle, inla should know what link function to apply.  Unfortunately, this interacts in a bad way with the way models with multiple likelihoods are implemented currently; for multiple likelihood, the data vector becomes a matrix, where each column corresponds to its own likelihood (and hence link function).  The problem is then that the "NA values" in the matrix are doing double duty; for each row, typically there would be either an NA in one column and an observation in the other, _or_ NA in both.  In the former case, the NA would normally mean "no data because this row of the model belongs to the other likelihood.  In the latter case, the same holds, but no the _other_ NA means "missing value", and inla has no way of knowing which is which.  In theory, inla could then just apply the link functions on _all_ NA values, but that could quickly run into practical and numerical difficulties due to different scaling etc.  Hence, inla leaves it to the user to apply the link functions corresponding to NA elements, since the user does know the meaning of each NA entry.

A more elegant solution would be to have separate formulas and data vectors for each likelihood, but that would be a major redesign of the code, and so that won't happen overnight...
But I've designed a way for the user to instead specify specifically which elements come from which likelihood; I'll discuss it with Håvard.

/Finn L

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, 21 March 2012 11:08:35 UTC+1, Laura Serra Saurina wrote:
> I would like to know the difference between the two types of zero-inflated models (type 0 and type 1). Looking at the formula I noticed that type 0 only includes positives values and type 1 includes all kind of values. Is there any other difference?
>
> Type 0: Prob(y|...) = p x 1[y=0] + (1 - p) x Poisson(y | y > 0)
>
> Type 1: Prob(y|...) = p x 1[y=0] + (1 - p) x Poisson(y)

Type 1 is a mixture of a point mass at 0 and a regular Poisson distribution, whereas Type 0 is a mixture of a truncated Poisson (the y>0 bit) and a point mass at 0, so that the probability at zero is governed directly by p.

This means e.g. that Type 0 can have a _lower_ probability at 0 than a pure Poisson, relative to the probability at 1, whereas Type 1 can only increase the relative probability for 0.

> Moreover, could you give me the Type2's formula? I haven't found it.

The description of Type 2 is at the end of page 6 of
http://www.math.ntnu.no/~hrue/r-inla.org/doc/likelihood/zeroinflated.pdf
It's like Type 1 but with a different definition of p.

/Finn

messages.subject_clean: Effect of scaling affects significance in joint Poisson model
messages.body_plain:
Dear list

My background is the joint analysis of four indicators for a target measure which is impossible to determine. The four indicators are all counts of certain properties but with different means and variance. We have observed the four indicators in grouped subjects.
I started to analyse this using a poisson GLMM just with all counts of the four indicators concatenated. However, I realised that the different means and variances are a problem. I could however get roughly similar distributions by dividing the original indicator values by their mean.
Second option is the use of a joint INLA model with four Poisson response variables. However, in a simulation example this standardisation completely messes up my significance in INLA. On the other hand, both INLA results agrees with the GLMM.
I am not a bit worried what really the right way of analysing is? Is it GLMM with standardisation, which suggests the treatment effect is not significant, OR is it INLA without standardisation, which suggests a significant treatment effect. Hope this gets clearer with the example:

##Start of code
#Generating dataset
set.seed(1234)
fixEff <- 0.1
fixInt <- 3
EffInd <- rnorm(4,fixEff,0.1)
IntInd <- rnorm(4,fixInt,1.5)
GrInt <- sapply(IntInd, function(x) rnorm(9, x, .1))
SubjInt <- rnorm(180, 0, .01)
logl <- rep(GrInt, each=20) + SubjInt + rep(rep(c(0,1), each=10),36)*rep(EffInd, each=180)
ysim <- sapply(exp(logl), function(x) rpois(1, lambda=x))
d3 <- data.frame(ysim = ysim, Subj=rep(1:180,4), Ind=rep(LETTERS[1:4], each=180),
            Gr =rep(letters[1:9],each=20), Treat=rep(rep(c(0,1), each=10),36))
d3$ysimS <- d3$ysim/rep(tapply(d3$ysim, d3$Ind, mean),each=180)

##Generating stacked Y for INLA (original and standardized)
Y <- Ys <- matrix(NA, 180*4, 4)
E <- rep(1, 180*4)
for(i in 1:4) Y[(1:180)+((i-1)*180), i] <- d3$ysim[(1:180)+((i-1)*180)]
for(i in 1:4) Ys[(1:180)+((i-1)*180), i] <- d3$ysimS[(1:180)+((i-1)*180)]

formula <- Y ~ 1 + Treat + f(Gr, model="iid") + f(Subj, model="iid")
M1 <- inla(formula, data=d3, family=rep("poisson",4), E=E)
summary(M1)
#Significant treatment effect

formula <- Ys ~ 1 + Treat + f(Gr, model="iid") + f(Subj, model="iid")
M1S <- inla(formula, data=d3, family=rep("poisson",4), E=E)
summary(M1S)

M2 <- lmer(ysim ~ 1 + Treat + (1|Subj) + (1|Gr), data=d3, family="poisson")
summary(M2)
#Significant treatment effect in agreement with INLA.

M2S <- lmer(ysimS ~ 1 + Treat + (1|Subj) + (1|Gr), data=d3, family="poisson")
summary(M2S)
##End of code.

My original model was M2 of which I was suspicious because my indicator with largest mean showed strongest treatment effect. However, maybe this is effectively a true effect.
OR: My INLA specification is not entirely correct and I can do something better.

Any comments and thoughts are highly appreciated.
Kind regards
Manuel

this topic has been discussed several times, at least internally. so,
what is there now, is a prototype:

inla.hyperpar.sampler(result)

that will sample from the joint of the hyperparameters, either in the
internal or user-scale. its currently undocumented, but as said, its a
prototype only, and it might change, as we're not sure what we really
want/need in this direction.

when you say 'sampling from the joint posterior'; its indeed possible
but not yet implemented. its not awfully hard to add, its just
administration mainly.

there are two strategies to provide samples. do we want samples for both
the hyperparameters (theta) and the latent field (x), as

1. for each theta-configuration used in the numerical integration,
provide N samples from x.

or

2. sample theta from its marginal and then for each theta-configuration,
sample a realisation of x.

?

option 1, can be done with mainly with no cost at all, as long as its
done in the same call, like

	result = inla(..., control.compute=list(nsamples = 100))

say [THIS IS JUST AN EXAMPLE!]

whereas option 2, would require a new run, and can be done after, like

	result = inla(...)
	my.samples = inla.sample(result, nsamples = 100)

and would cost quite a lot compared to option 1.

option 1, has also the benefite, that we could correct samples using
their marginals, so we're using a Gaussian copula and correct with the
computed marginals. whereas option 2, the same idea would be costly, as
we do not want to recompute the marginals and only the mixture is
stored, so with option 2 we're ending up sampling just the Gaussian's.

any ideas ?
